questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a letter to an old friend (about 100 words) telling her why you have started keeping a diary and why you have given your notebook a name.

markingPoints.description: Content: explains that she talks to her friends only about ordinary everyday things and that nobody gets any closer. (1)
Content: says the diary is to be her friend instead of a bare record of facts, and gives it the name 'Kitty'. (1)
Format: a letter, with a greeting, the body in paragraphs and a suitable closing. (1)
Organisation: the reason and the plan are given in a clear, connected order. (1)
Accuracy and expression: correct spelling, grammar and punctuation in a friendly tone. (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Dear Sunita,
All I think about when I am with my friends is having a good time. I cannot bring myself to talk about anything but ordinary everyday things, and we do not seem to be able to get any closer. That is why I have started a diary. I do not want to jot down facts the way most people do; I want the diary to be my friend, so I have called it ‘Kitty’. On paper I can say all the things I have kept off my chest.
Write back soon.
Yours,
Meera

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a speech (about 100 words) to be delivered in your school assembly on why students should keep a diary.

markingPoints.description: Content: gives the first reason — the writer seems to have everything, yet has nobody she can confide in. (1)
Content: gives the second reason — paper has more patience than people and will listen without getting bored. (1)
Format: a speech, with a greeting to the audience and a short closing. (1)
Organisation: opening, then the reasons in order, then a conclusion with advice. (1)
Accuracy and expression: correct grammar and a formal, clear voice suited to an assembly. (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Good morning, everyone. I want to speak to you about keeping a diary. Many of us have about thirty people we can call friends, and yet we speak to them only about ordinary everyday things. Paper has more patience than people. A notebook will not laugh at you, and it will listen to your worries without getting bored. So take a quiet half hour each evening and write honestly, and you will find that the thoughts you could not tell a friend are safely on paper. Start with one line about your day and go on from there. Thank you.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Subject: Request for help with talking too much in class
Dear Sir,
I am writing to ask for your help. I know that I talk far too much in class, and I know that you have every reason to be annoyed with me. When my friends are behind me I get carried away and forget that the lesson is still going on. I once wrote three pages arguing that talking is a student’s trait, but I could not keep quiet in the very next lesson. Could you suggest something I can use when I feel the urge to speak? I promise to follow it.
Yours sincerely,
Ishaan

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Mr Keesing punishes Anne again and again for talking far too much in class; set out, in steps, how three essays change his mind and win back her right to talk.

markingPoints.description: Step 1: Mr Keesing, the old fogey who teaches maths, was annoyed with her for ages because she talked so much, and after several warnings assigned extra homework (1)
Step 2: the first essay was on ‘A Chatterbox’; she wrote three pages arguing that talking is a student’s trait (1)
Step 3: she adds that she would never be able to cure the habit, because her mother talks as much as she does and it is an inherited trait (1)
Step 4: he laughs at her arguments, but when she talks her way through the next lesson he assigns a second essay, on ‘An Incorrigible Chatterbox’ (1)
Step 5: in the third lesson he has finally had enough and orders her to write ‘Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox’ (1)
Step 6: Sanne helps her write it in verse; he takes the joke the right way, reads it to the class and to several other classes, and she is then allowed to talk with no extra homework (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Annoyed — Mr Keesing, the old fogey who teaches maths, was annoyed with her for ages because she talked so much, and after several warnings assigned extra homework.
2. First essay — the subject was ‘A Chatterbox’. She wrote three pages and argued that talking is a student’s trait.
3. Her excuse — she would never be able to cure the habit, since her mother talks as much as she does.
4. Second essay — he laughed, but when she talked her way through the next lesson he assigned one on ‘An Incorrigible Chatterbox’.
5. Third punishment — in the third lesson he had finally had enough and ordered ‘Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox’.
6. He accepts her — Sanne wrote it in verse, he took the joke the right way, and she was then allowed to talk with no extra homework.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Set out, in steps, the events in Anne’s family life that carry her from Frankfurt to the solemn dedication of her diary on 20 June 1942.

markingPoints.description: Step 1: her father emigrated to Holland in 1933, and her mother, Edith Hollander Frank, went with him in September (1)
Step 2: Margot and Anne were sent to Aachen to stay with their grandmother; Margot went to Holland in December and Anne followed in February (1)
Step 3: Anne went as a birthday present for Margot, and started at the Montessori nursery school, staying until she was six (1)
Step 4: in the sixth form her teacher was Mrs Kuperus, the headmistress, and at the end of the year the two said a heartbreaking farewell (1)
Step 5: in the summer of 1941 Grandma fell ill and had to have an operation, so Anne’s birthday passed with little celebration, and Grandma died in January 1942 (1)

Step 6: the 1942 celebration was meant to make up for that one, with Grandma’s candle lit along with the rest, and on 20 June 1942 the four of them were still doing well, so the diary is solemnly dedicated (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. 1933 — her father emigrated to Holland, and her mother Edith Hollander Frank went with him in September.
2. Margot and Anne were sent to Aachen to stay with their grandmother. Margot went to Holland in December; Anne followed in February.
3. Anne was a birthday present for Margot, and she started at the Montessori nursery school until she was six.
4. In the sixth form her teacher was Mrs Kuperus, the headmistress, and at the year’s end they said a heartbreaking farewell.
5. In the summer of 1941 Grandma fell ill and had an operation; she died in January 1942, and Anne’s 1942 birthday made up for the last one.
6. Grandma’s candle was lit along with the rest, and on 20 June 1942 the four of them were still doing well, so the diary is solemnly dedicated.
